summary: In IPv6, the Fragment Header carries an Identification field that helps a receiver match fragments of the same original packet. This informational RFC examines the security problems that arise when those values are predictable, such as enabling attackers to interfere with traffic, and discusses how implementations should generate them.

eli5.summary: When a big package is sent in pieces, each piece has a number tag. If an attacker can guess the tags, they can sneak in fake pieces, so the tags should be hard to guess.

questions: why are predictable fragment ids a security problem
what algorithms should generate ipv6 fragment ids
how do fragment injection attacks work
subtitle: Why IPv6 fragment IDs must not be predictable

tldr.problem: IPv6 uses an Identification field to match fragments belonging to the same original packet so they can be reassembled. If this field is predictable, attackers can inject fake fragments or interfere with legitimate communication.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes how predictable Identification values enable various attacks, and describes three algorithms (per-destination counter, randomized values, and hash-based selection) that implementations should use instead of simple global counters.
tldr.outcome: It provides concrete guidance for IPv6 implementations to generate Identification values that are hard to predict while meeting reassembly requirements and maintaining good performance.

today: RFC 7739 remains an informational RFC providing security guidance to IPv6 implementers. While it does not mandate changes, it documents known vulnerabilities in simple counter-based ID generation. Modern IPv6 stacks generally use better algorithms, but legacy systems and older implementations may remain vulnerable. Network operators should verify that systems in their deployments generate unpredictable fragment IDs.

sections.title: The Fragment Identification Problem
sections.content:
IPv6 uses a Fragment Header to split large packets into smaller pieces for transmission over networks with size limits. The Fragment Header contains an Identification field that, together with the source and destination addresses, uniquely identifies fragments belonging to the same original datagram. The receiving host uses this information to reassemble fragments in the correct order.

The IPv6 specification (RFC 2460) only requires that Identification values be different from those used recently with the same source and destination addresses. However, some implementations use a simple global counter—starting at zero and incrementing for each fragmented packet. This approach is fast but results in predictable Identification values that can be exploited. The RFC examines why this is a security problem and recommends better algorithms.
sections.eli5: IPv6 splits big messages into pieces and labels each piece with a number. The receiver uses the label to put pieces back together. Simple implementations just count 1, 2, 3, 4... which is easy to predict.

sections.title: How Predictable IDs Enable Attacks
sections.content:
Predictable Identification values leak information that attackers can exploit in multiple ways. An attacker can use them to determine how fast a system is transmitting data, perform stealth port scans against third parties, uncover firewall rules, count the number of devices behind a middle-box, perform denial-of-service attacks, or even inject data into upper-layer protocols. These attack vectors were first documented for IPv4 and apply similarly to IPv6.

One key difference in IPv6 is that the Fragment Header is only present in fragmented packets, not all packets. An attacker must first force the victim to fragment packets (for example, by sending forged ICMPv6 messages claiming the path MTU is too small). However, many IPv6 implementations fail to properly validate these ICMPv6 messages, making them vulnerable to such attacks. Once fragmentation is triggered, predictable Identification values enable the attacker to craft forged fragments that collide with legitimate fragments or replace them entirely.
sections.eli5: If you know what label the next packet will have, you can send a fake packet with the same label and confuse the receiver. The attacker can trick a system into fragmenting its packets, then send fake pieces, and the receiver cannot tell which pieces are real.

sections.title: Three Better Algorithms
sections.content:
The RFC describes three algorithms for generating Identification values that are hard to predict. The first is a per-destination counter: maintain a separate counter for each destination address, initialized to a random value. For each fragmented packet to that destination, increment the counter by one. This gives good performance (just incrementing a counter) and reasonable security (the attacker cannot predict values without knowing the initial random value). A drawback is that if the destination cache entry is removed due to memory pressure, the counter is lost and might cause collisions.

The second algorithm uses fully randomized Identification values: select each Identification from a pseudorandom number generator. This is the simplest to understand and securely unpredictable, but uses a PRNG for every fragmented packet, which is slower. The third algorithm is hash-based selection: compute an unpredictable offset using a hash of the source and destination addresses and a secret, then add a monotonically increasing counter. This achieves good performance without losing state, and is useful when a system fragments traffic to many destinations.
sections.eli5: Better approach 1: keep a separate random counter for each place you send to. Better approach 2: pick a random number each time. Better approach 3: use a secret formula plus a counter so the attacker cannot predict it even if they see many packets.

sections.title: Implementation Constraints and Trade-offs
sections.content:
Implementers must balance security with performance and interoperability. The Identification field is 32 bits long, but when IPv4/IPv6 translators are used, only the lower 16 bits are preserved. So for maximum compatibility, implementations should assume only 16 bits of Identification space are reliable. Additionally, the only hard requirement from RFC 2460 is that Identification values not be reused recently with the same source and destination; violating this can cause reassembly failures.

Each of the three algorithms makes different trade-offs. Per-destination counters are fast but require per-destination state. Randomized values are unconditionally unpredictable but slower. Hash-based selection is a middle ground: reasonably fast, no per-destination state needed, and unpredictable (though not unconditionally). The choice depends on whether the implementation cares more about memory efficiency, CPU speed, or absolute security.
sections.eli5: There is a choice between memory, speed and perfect security. If you have lots of destinations, keep counters; if you need to be fastest, use random; if you want balance, use the hash method.

sections.title: Status and Recommendations
sections.content:
This RFC is informational; it recommends but does not require implementers to use the proposed algorithms. Many existing IPv6 implementations were surveyed and found to use predictable Identification values. The RFC includes an appendix examining several popular implementations and showing vulnerabilities in their approaches. The hope is that implementers will adopt one of the three recommended algorithms to improve security.

The RFC notes that this is a significant change from simple global counters that existing implementations might use, but the performance impact should be acceptable for most deployments. Operations teams should verify that their systems generate unpredictable Identification values, especially if their network involves IPv6 fragmentation (which, while less common than IPv4 fragmentation historically, can occur due to ICMPv6 messages or large protocol extensions).
sections.eli5: This is a suggestion, not a rule, so old systems might not follow it yet. But hackers can exploit old systems, so network operators should check if their routers and computers generate random-looking fragment ID numbers.

left.title: Vulnerable: Simple Counter
left.desc: Uses global counter (0, 1, 2, 3...). Attacker can predict the next ID value and craft forged fragments.

right.title: Secure: Randomized Values
right.desc: Uses cryptographic randomness or per-destination random initialization. Attacker cannot predict the next ID.
